title: Convection
lead: Convection is heat carried by matter that moves: air that a furnace has warmed rises because it has become less dense, water at the bottom of a pot rises for the same reason, and the wind, the oceans and the atmosphere carry heat the same way on a larger scale. This section shows how to calculate the heat a moving mass of fluid carries, why a cold wind chills far more than still air at the same temperature, why fur and double-paned windows insulate by trapping air that cannot move, and how much more heat convection carries when the moving fluid evaporates or condenses along the way.
objectives: Discuss the method of heat transfer by convection.
summary_html: • Convection is heat transfer by the macroscopic movement of mass. Convection can be natural or forced and generally transfers thermal energy faster than conduction. Table 14.4 gives wind-chill factors, indicating that moving air has the same chilling effect of much colder stationary air. Convection that occurs along with a phase change can transfer energy from cold regions to warm ones.

figures.original_caption: Air heated by the so-called gravity furnace expands and rises, forming a convective loop that transfers energy to other parts of the room. As the air is cooled at the ceiling and outside walls, it contracts, eventually becoming denser than room air and sinking to the floor. A properly designed heating system using natural convection, like this one, can be quite efficient in uniformly heating a home. (Figure 14.22) Convection plays an important role in heat transfer inside this pot of water. Once conducted to the inside, heat transfer to other parts of the pot is mostly by convection. The hotter water expands, decreases in density, and rises to transfer heat to other regions of the water, while colder water sinks to the bottom. This process keeps repeating.
Fur is filled with air, breaking it up into many small pockets. Convection is very slow here, because the loops are so small. The low conductivity of air makes fur a very good lightweight insulator.

exercises.prompt: Explain why using a fan in the summer feels refreshing!

answer.solution: Using a fan increases the flow of air: warm air near your body is replaced by cooler air from elsewhere. Convection increases the rate of heat transfer so that moving air “feels” cooler than still air.

exercises.prompt: Under which two conditions would convection in a fluid be greatest?

options: The gravitational acceleration is large, and the fluid density varies greatly for a given temperature change.
The gravitational acceleration is small, and the fluid density varies greatly for a given temperature change.
The gravitational acceleration is large, and the fluid density varies slightly for a given temperature change.
The gravitational acceleration is small, and the fluid density varies slightly for a given temperature change.
answer.hint: Natural convection is driven by the buoyant force on the warmed fluid, and the buoyant force is the weight of the denser fluid the warmed fluid displaces, less its own weight.

exercises.prompt: Sea breezes occur along coastlines, and consist of cool air moving toward the shore from the ocean. However, this only occurs during the day, and is a stronger effect when the air temperature on the land is greatest and the air temperature above the water is coldest. At night, the breezes are reversed, moving from the land toward the ocean. Taking into consideration the specific heat capacities of water and sand (which is about the same as that of concrete), explain how sea breezes form during the day and change direction at night.

answer.solution: Water has a specific heat about five times that of sand or concrete, so for the same heat transfer from the Sun the land warms far more than the sea does. During the day the air over the land is warmed by the hot ground, expands and becomes less dense, and the cooler, denser air over the water flows in beneath it and pushes it up: that inflow is the sea breeze, and it is strongest when the land is hottest and the water coldest, since the density difference that drives it is then largest. At night the land, with its small specific heat, cools quickly while the water, with its large specific heat, stays nearly as warm as it was, so the air over the water is now the warmer and lighter air, it rises, and the cooler air from the land flows out to take its place. The breeze is the same convective loop as the room heated by a gravity furnace, with the warmer surface playing the part of the furnace, and it reverses when the warmer surface changes from the land to the sea.

exercises.prompt: One way to make a fireplace more energy efficient is to have an external air supply for the combustion of its fuel. Another is to have room air circulate around the outside of the fire box and back into the room. Detail the methods of heat transfer involved in each.

answer.solution: A fire draws air for combustion and sends it up the chimney, and in an ordinary fireplace that air is the room’s warm air, so the room is emptied of warm air by forced convection up the chimney and refilled by cold air drawn in around the doors and windows, the very leakage of Example 14.7. An external air supply feeds the fire with outside air instead, so the warm air of the room is not carried away, and the room keeps the heat that reaches it from the fire by radiation through the opening and by conduction through the fire box. Circulating room air around the outside of the fire box adds convection working for the room rather than against it: heat is conducted through the wall of the fire box into the air passing over it, that warmed air expands, becomes less dense and rises back into the room, and cooler room air flows in beneath to be warmed in its turn, so a convective loop carries heat from the hot metal into the room instead of letting it go up the chimney.

exercises.prompt: On cold, clear nights horses will sleep under the cover of large trees. How does this help them keep warm?

answer.solution: The branches and leaves of a large tree slow the wind, and the air beneath them is far stiller than the air in an open field. A horse standing in a wind loses heat by convection, as the wind-chill factors of Table 14.4 show, because the moving air carries away the air the horse’s body has warmed and replaces it with cold air; under the tree the warmed air stays near the horse, and heat leaves it only by conduction through nearly still air, which is a poor conductor. The cover also shields the horse from the clear night sky, to which an animal in the open loses heat by radiation, the method of the next section, so the horse under the tree loses heat more slowly by both methods.

exercises.prompt: At what wind speed does $-10^\circ\text{C}$ air cause the same chill factor as still air at $-29^\circ\text{C}$?

answer.hint: Find the row of Table 14.4 for moving air at −10 °C and read across it for the entry −29 °C.

exercises.prompt: The “steam” above a freshly made cup of instant coffee is really water vapor droplets condensing after evaporating from the hot coffee. What is the final temperature of 250 g of hot coffee initially at $90.0^\circ\text{C}$ if 2.00 g evaporates from it? The coffee is in a Styrofoam cup, so other methods of heat transfer can be neglected.

answer.hint: The heat that evaporates the 2.00 g, $\kQh = mL_{\text{v}}$ with the heat of vaporization at the coffee’s temperature, comes out of the remaining coffee, whose temperature falls by $\kdTemp = \kQh/mc$.

exercises.prompt: On a hot dry day, evaporation from a lake has just enough heat transfer to balance the $1.00\ \text{kW/m}^2$ of incoming heat from the Sun. What mass of water evaporates in 1.00 h from each square meter? Explicitly show how you follow the steps in the Problem-Solving Strategies for the Effects of Heat Transfer.

answer.hint: In 1.00 h each square meter receives $\kQh = (1000\ \text{W})(3600\ \text{s})$ of heat, and evaporation must carry all of it away, so $m = \kQh/L_{\text{v}}$ with the heat of vaporization of water at the lake’s temperature.

exercises.prompt: The Kilauea volcano in Hawaii is the world’s most active, disgorging about $5 \times 10^{5}\ \text{m}^3$ of $1200^\circ\text{C}$ lava per day. What is the rate of heat transfer out of Earth by convection if this lava has a density of $2700\ \text{kg/m}^3$ and eventually cools to $30^\circ\text{C}$? Assume that the specific heat of lava is the same as that of granite.

answer.hint: The mass moved each day is $m = \krho V$; the heat it gives up in cooling is $\kQh = mc\kdTemp$ with granite’s specific heat from Table 14.1; and the rate is that heat divided by the seconds in a day.

exercises.prompt: A person inhales and exhales 2.00 L of $37.0^\circ\text{C}$ air, evaporating $4.00 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{g}$ of water from the lungs and breathing passages with each breath. (a) How much heat transfer occurs due to evaporation in each breath? (b) What is the rate of heat transfer in watts if the person is breathing at a moderate rate of 18.0 breaths per minute? (c) If the inhaled air had a temperature of $20.0^\circ\text{C}$, what is the rate of heat transfer for warming the air? (d) Discuss the total rate of heat transfer as it relates to typical metabolic rates. Will this breathing be a major form of heat transfer for this person?

parts.hint: The heat is $\kQh = mL_{\text{v}}$ with the heat of vaporization of water at body temperature, 2430 kJ/kg.
Eighteen breaths a minute is 0.300 breaths a second; multiply the heat of one breath by that rate.

The mass of 2.00 L of air follows from its density, 1.29 kg/m³; the heat to warm it by 17.0 °C is $\kQh = mc\kdTemp$ with the specific heat of air at constant pressure, and the rate is that heat times the breathing rate.

answer.solution: (a) 97.2 J (b) 29.2 W (c) 9.49 W (d) The total rate of heat loss would be $29.2\ \text{W} + 9.49\ \text{W} = 38.7\ \text{W}$. While sleeping, our body consumes 83 W of power, while sitting it consumes 120 to 210 W. Therefore, the total rate of heat loss from breathing will not be a major form of heat loss for this person.
